search_branch: finite-sample certification and conformal per-instance uncertainty

candidates.mechanism: Treat LLM-judge outputs as noisy labels, estimate judge true-positive and false-positive rates from a small human calibration set, and apply a variance-corrected hypothesis test to a large judge-labeled set so certification retains finite-sample Type-I error control.

evidence.source: Noisy but Valid: Robust Statistical Evaluation of LLMs with Imperfect Judges
evidence.quantitative_or_formal: The method estimates judge TPR/FPR from a small human-labeled calibration set, uses a variance-corrected critical threshold, and provides finite-sample Type-I error control despite calibration uncertainty. The paper derives conditions under which noisy testing has higher power than direct evaluation and validates on Jigsaw Comment, Hate Speech, and SafeRLHF; it also reports a practical-vs-oracle gap caused by estimating judge parameters.

candidates.interpretation: This supplies a principled statistical layer missing from heuristic judge-validation gates. The judge is explicitly modeled as an imperfect sensor rather than assumed correct. A small amount of trusted human data can anchor large-scale judge evaluation while preserving a chosen false-certification error rate.
candidates.connection_to_mvvp: MVVP can screen whether a judge is stable/invariant/cross-benchmark valid enough to use; Noisy-but-Valid can then propagate its residual TPR/FPR uncertainty into population-level certification. These solve different layers and are complementary.
candidates.scope_limits: Binary failure labels and certification of a population failure rate; extension to ordinal/multi-class/open-ended scoring requires separate theory. Judge TPR/FPR may drift across target-model distributions, so calibration-transfer stability remains a critical assumption.

candidates.mechanism: Use split conformal prediction sets/intervals around judge outputs to expose per-instance ambiguity with finite-sample coverage guarantees rather than relying only on aggregate judge reliability.

evidence.source: Diagnosing LLM Judge Reliability: Conformal Prediction Sets and Transitivity Violations
evidence.quantitative: On SummEval, aggregate transitivity-violation rates were only 0.8-4.1%, yet 33-67% of documents had at least one directed 3-cycle. Split conformal sets over 1-5 scores provided >=(1-alpha) coverage; set width correlated with per-instance disagreement/difficulty (Spearman r=+0.576, N=1,918, p<1e-100), with cross-judge set-width correlations around 0.32-0.38.

candidates.interpretation: Aggregate metrics can hide local inconsistency. Conformal set width is a usable abstention/escalation signal: wide sets identify items where a point judge score should not be trusted.
candidates.scope_limits: SummEval/rating setup; requires exchangeability for formal coverage and calibrated labeled data. Transitivity analysis applies naturally to pairwise/ranking settings but not every evaluation task.

proposed_evaluation_stack: Layer 1 construct validity: objective/checkable benchmarks where possible plus preference-style benchmark coverage.
Layer 2 judge diagnostics: chance-corrected agreement, AB/BA invariance, >=3 replicate consistency, cross-benchmark stability.
Layer 3 judge-noise model: estimate TPR/FPR or calibrated success probabilities on target-distribution holdout data.
Layer 4 statistical inference: finite-sample noisy-judge hypothesis tests for population claims/certification.
Layer 5 per-instance uncertainty: conformal sets or calibrated confidence; abstain/escalate high-uncertainty items.
Layer 6 ensemble diversity: measure error correlation/effective sample size before adding judges.
new_synthesis.why_it_matters: The literature increasingly separates three quantities that are often conflated: repeatability, correctness/validity, and uncertainty. A robust evaluator should preserve them as separate measured objects rather than compressing them into one judge score.

frontier_queue.question: Extract numerical power/sample-size tradeoffs and the practical-vs-oracle gap from Noisy but Valid; determine minimum human calibration size as a function of judge TPR/FPR, target failure threshold, and desired Type-I/II error.

Compare Noisy-but-Valid against prediction-powered inference and the ICLR 2026 constrained-MLE follow-up under calibration transfer/mismatch; identify which method fails most gracefully when judge TPR/FPR shifts across candidate models.
Connect conformal set width to routing policies: human review, stronger judge, tool-based verifier, or extra test-time compute; measure risk-coverage curves instead of accuracy alone.
Check whether conformal guarantees survive correlated judge panels or repeated samples from the same foundation model; quantify exchangeability violations and effective calibration size.
Search objective agentic-trajectory and code/math evaluation benchmarks where this full stack can be tested end-to-end with ground-truth execution signals.

termination_diagnostics.completed_unresolved_action: Followed the MVVP statistical-guarantee frontier into ICLR 2026 finite-sample noisy-judge certification and a 2026 conformal per-instance reliability diagnostic.
termination_diagnostics.exact_next_action: Read arXiv:2601.20913 full text and extract its finite-sample critical-threshold formula, power conditions, calibration-set sizes, and empirical oracle-gap numbers; then compare them to constrained-MLE/PPI alternatives under TPR/FPR mismatch.
